1. Research role: Detector evidence: human-vs-agent and agent-family fingerprinting
2. Interface / environment: Controlled honey website: flight booking, shopping, and forum interaction
3. Observer position: First-party page instrumentation with server-side storage
4. Observable signal: 418 browser-fingerprint and 50 behavior features; key, mouse, scroll, paste, and change events
5. Action / architecture: Seven browsing agents plus humans; XGBoost on browser-only, behavior-only, and combined features
6. Unit / horizon: One task trial; 1,000 trials per agent; 56 humans completed 3 tasks x 3 repetitions

Key result: Agents+human macro-F1 is 0.8223 browser-only, 0.9994 behavior-only, and 1.0000 combined (Table 2)

Project-design consequence: Capture behavior and missing modalities separately from browser metadata; evaluate held-out tasks and agent families; treat human collection as human-subjects work

1. Research role: Attribution evidence after automation has already been detected
2. Interface / environment: Live tasks from 2Wiki, FRAMES, WebShop, and DeepShop
4. Observable signal: 41 scalar features from click, keydown, scroll, navigation, unload, focus, and timing
5. Action / architecture: Fourteen LLM browser agents through MidScene/PlaywrightAgent in headless Chromium
6. Unit / horizon: One session trace; 1,050 runs split 525/262/263; 40 cycles or 300 seconds
7. Evaluation protocol: Closed-set, open-set, delay-adapted, cross-task, pooled-site, and cross-site tests
Key result: Closed-set per-agent F1 is mostly above 0.70 and reaches 0.96; performance is roughly 10x chance (Figure 2)

Project-design consequence: Separate detection from attribution; add timing perturbation and task/site holdouts; never let site or task identifiers enter detector features

2. Interface / environment: 108 long-horizon tasks spanning 31 websites and desktop applications

1. Research role: Evaluation-validity warning for live web-agent experiments
2. Interface / environment: Live websites and six web agents evaluated with human annotations and WebJudge
3. Observer position: Trajectory evaluator using screenshots and actions rather than the agent's final claim alone
4. Observable signal: Intermediate screenshots, actions, final state, and optional final response

Key result: Human-evaluated success is 30.0% for Browser Use and 61.3% for Operator (Table 2)

1. Research role: Active-challenge detector evidence for survey-taking agents; complementary to passive behavioral biometrics
2. Interface / environment: Qualtrics browser survey with Prolific humans and four vision-agent platforms; MTurk and CloudResearch Connect replications
3. Observer position: Survey instrument scores response correctness and decision timing; it does not observe raw OS or browser events
4. Observable signal: Six randomized visual-trap outcomes, per-item discrimination, choice-page decision time, attention checks, and CAPTCHA comparator
5. Action / architecture: Vision-enabled agents capture screenshots, reason over rendered questions, and submit responses; validation spans 34 VLMs and four deployed agent platforms
6. Unit / horizon: One approximately seven-minute survey session; six traps; 1,007 Prolific humans and 526 deployed agents in the main validation
7. Evaluation protocol: Trap retention on 202 humans and six models; expanded 34-model/2,040-trial validation; main deployment threshold selected from validation data, then preregistered for MTurk and Connect replications
Key result: Failing at least three of six traps detected 511/526 agents (97.1%) while flagging 41/1,007 presumed humans (4.1%); traditional checks detected 2.3% of agents
8. Failure / claim boundary: Active challenge rather than passive trace detection; assumed human ground truth, visual-accessibility risk, platform heterogeneity, model drift, and no direct behavioral-biometric comparison
Project-design consequence: Treat active cognitive traps as a future complementary channel, not a replacement for event traces; calibrate thresholds on an independent population and keep response content out of the passive detector
Evidence locator: Cognitive Trap Framework; Human/Initial/Expanded Model Validation; Figure 2; Tables 2-4; Prolific Method/Results; Practical Recommendations; Limitations

1. Research role: Agent-as-attacker characterization and active website defense; not a detector benchmark
2. Interface / environment: 237 offline snapshots from 50 websites with 10,895 annotated images; L2S, LNC, and LWA scraper paradigms
3. Observer position: Website owner and benchmark harness with ground-truth target-asset URLs
4. Observable signal: Extracted asset URLs, recall/precision, execution time, token/CPU/memory overhead, input modality, and protected-page condition
5. Action / architecture: Parse-then-interpret scrapers; Browser-Use combines UI and DOM while UI-only agents act visually; WebCloak applies structural obfuscation plus semantic labyrinth
6. Unit / horizon: One page-level extraction episode; 32 scraper variants for measurement and three representative systems on the full benchmark
7. Evaluation protocol: Offline protected/unprotected comparison, adaptive-attack checks, browser/OS checks, and N=35 usability study; benchmark-wide defense evaluation rather than a detector split
Key result: Browser-Use reached 60.4% recall and 88.8% precision without defense; full WebCloak reduced average evaluated-agent recall from 88.7% to 0%
8. Failure / claim boundary: Image-centric benchmark, smaller text/audio check, JavaScript-dependent restoration, and novice-to-intermediate threat model; disruption does not identify who produced a session
Project-design consequence: Audit DOM/visual executor and page condition as provenance, exclude them from detector features, and test recorder coverage under adversarial DOM changes before interpreting missing events as actor behavior

1. Research role: External intervention and corrigibility benchmark; threat evidence rather than actor detection
2. Interface / environment: WebArena-derived multi-step browser tasks across eight harmful scenarios and seven sites
3. Observer position: External harness observes signal encounter, terminal/refusal behavior, and subsequent task progression
4. Observable signal: ISR, KSR, KSRcond, PSR, ASR, terminal actions, and post-signal continuation; benchmark-only chain-of-thought cause
5. Action / architecture: C1 text, C2 system-prompt-bypass, C3 multimodal, and C4 uncensored agents over BrowserGym/AgentLab; four external payload defenses
6. Unit / horizon: One multi-step trajectory with payload placed on the second page; 550 prompts from ten jailbreak patterns
7. Evaluation protocol: No-s baseline and four defenses across configurations/backbones, with per-scenario and per-pattern analysis; no detector train/test split
Key result: AUTOGUARD averages 43.5% KSRcond and exceeds 88% on aligned GPT-5.2 C1/C3, while C2/C4 remain difficult and GCG averages 2.8%
8. Failure / claim boundary: ASR measures failure to halt, not real-world harm success; payload perturbation is not causally separated from halt; one Table 7 cell has an unrecoverable logging inconsistency
Project-design consequence: Represent refusal, stop, timeout, and validator outcome separately; keep post-stop negative controls and termination timing, but do not reproduce harmful scenarios or ingest action text
Evidence locator: Sections 4.1-4.3, 5.1-5.3, 6-7, and Limitations; Figures 1-5; Tables 1-4 and 6-8; Appendix A.7-A.10

1. Research role: Long-horizon agentic-search benchmark and partial-progress evaluator
2. Interface / environment: Live web search across 130 tasks, six domains, and 24 subdomains; answers require citations and time-varying information
3. Observer position: Judge agent consumes final answer, cited URLs, and cached webpage evidence
4. Observable signal: Rubric-node completion, full success, Pass@3, citations, cached pages, elapsed time, and answer length; no low-level interaction events
5. Action / architecture: Search products, Deep Research systems, and direct-browser Operator; some systems combine search, browser interaction, and code tools
6. Unit / horizon: One long-horizon task answer; average human task uses 18 minutes, eight websites, and 110 pages on Subset-30; three runs per agent system
7. Evaluation protocol: 10-task development and 120-task test split; three runs per system; randomly selected Subset-30 human study; cached-webpage judging and human audit
Key result: OpenAI Deep Research scored 0.54 partial completion, 0.28 full success, and 0.40 Pass@3; humans scored 0.79, 0.54, and 0.83 on Subset-30
8. Failure / claim boundary: Final-answer benchmark rather than trace dataset; live-page drift, cache failures, login/CAPTCHA barriers, closed systems, and a large partial/full-success gap
Project-design consequence: Version task and cached evidence, retain graded progress, and record low-level events separately; do not use final-answer metrics as evidence that the extension captured an agent

1. Research role: Hard-search capability benchmark and contamination-control reference; not a recorder or actor detector
2. Interface / environment: Open-web search questions with short, entangled-information answers; tool and executor are not standardized
3. Observer position: Final-answer evaluator holding an encrypted reference answer and using a semantic grader
4. Observable signal: Generated explanation, exact answer, confidence, and correctness; no standardized browser events or action path
5. Action / architecture: Any internet-enabled model or browsing agent; paper compares non-browsing, search-enabled, and Deep Research systems
6. Unit / horizon: One question-answer episode; 1,266 tasks; 64 samples per question in repeated-trial analyses; human search can last roughly two hours
7. Evaluation protocol: Official encrypted test-set evaluation with semantic answer matching; deterministic seed-0 optional subsampling; no benchmark training split
Key result: Deep Research achieved 51.5% accuracy; humans solved 29.2% of 1,255 attempted questions and agreed with the reference on 86.4% of solved cases
8. Failure / claim boundary: Short-answer proxy omits real user-query ambiguity, may have alternate valid answers, is leakage-sensitive, and uses a model grader; 21 problematic tasks were removed after zero-pass review
Project-design consequence: Do not use BrowseComp as the matched mouse/keyboard protocol; preserve its canary and never publish decrypted items, and treat any use as outcome-only capability evidence
Evidence locator: Sections 2.1-2.4, 3, and 4.1-4.5; Tables 2-3; Figures 1 and 3-5; Appendix B; official simple-evals browsecomp_eval.py
